name: chemistry_set3_p1
label: Chemistry: set 3 (non-metals, metals and industrial chemistry)

papers.title: Hydrogen: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on hydrogen, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Hydrogen is usually prepared in the laboratory by the action of
questions.explanation:
Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. A few drops of copper(II) sulphate speed up the reaction.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- dilute hydrochloric acid on copper turnings: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series and does not react.
- concentrated nitric acid on zinc: Nitric acid is an oxidising acid; it gives oxides of nitrogen, not hydrogen.
- water on sodium: The reaction is too violent to control safely.

options.label: A
options.content: dilute hydrochloric acid on copper turnings

options.label: C
options.content: dilute hydrochloric acid on zinc granules

questions.stem: Hydrogen can be collected over water because it is
questions.explanation:
A gas is collected over water if it does not dissolve in or react with water.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- lighter than air: Being lighter than air allows upward delivery, not collection over water.
- a reducing agent: Reducing power has nothing to do with the collection method.
- colourless: Colour does not decide the collection method.

questions.stem: Which observation identifies hydrogen gas?
questions.explanation:
A small amount of hydrogen mixed with air explodes gently: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- It relights a glowing splint: That is the test for oxygen.
- It turns lime water milky: That is the test for carbon(IV) oxide.
- It turns damp red litmus paper blue: That is the test for ammonia.

options.label: C
options.content: It burns with a squeaky pop when a lighted splint is applied

options.label: D
options.content: It turns damp red litmus paper blue

questions.stem: When dry hydrogen is passed over heated copper(II) oxide, the black solid
questions.explanation:
CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. Hydrogen is a reducing agent: it removes oxygen from the oxide.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- turns white and oxygen is given off: Copper(II) oxide is reduced, not decomposed; no oxygen is released.
- turns blue and hydrogen is absorbed: The product is copper metal, which is reddish-brown.
- does not change: Hydrogen reduces the oxides of metals below iron in the reactivity series.

options.label: A
options.content: turns white and oxygen is given off

options.label: B
options.content: turns blue and hydrogen is absorbed

options.label: D
options.content: turns reddish-brown and droplets of water form

questions.stem: What volume of hydrogen at s.t.p. is produced when 6.5 g of zinc reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid? Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
questions.explanation:
Moles Zn $= \dfrac{6.5}{65} = 0.1$; moles H₂ $= 0.1$; volume $= 0.1 \times 22.4 = 2.24$ dm³

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4.48 dm³: You used the 2 from 2HCl; 1 mol of zinc gives 1 mol of hydrogen.
- 145.6 dm³: You multiplied the mass by 22.4 without finding moles.
- 2.4 dm³: You used 24 dm³, the molar volume at room conditions.

papers.title: Oxygen and Air: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on oxygen and air, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which method is used to prepare oxygen in the laboratory?
questions.explanation:
2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. The MnO₂ is unchanged at the end; the oxygen is collected over water.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Heating calcium carbonate: Calcium carbonate gives carbon(IV) oxide.
- Adding zinc to dilute hydrochloric acid: This gives hydrogen.
- Heating ammonium chloride: This gives ammonia and hydrogen chloride.

options.label: B
options.content: Decomposing hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide as catalyst

options.label: C
options.content: Adding zinc to dilute hydrochloric acid

questions.stem: 100 cm³ of air is passed repeatedly over heated copper until the volume stops changing. 79 cm³ of gas remains. What is the percentage of oxygen in the air?
questions.explanation:
Oxygen removed $= 100 - 79 = 21$ cm³, so $\% \text{O}_2 = \dfrac{21}{100} \times 100 = 21\%$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 79%: That is the percentage of the gas left (mainly nitrogen).
- 100%: That is the total volume of air.
- 26.58%: You divided by the volume remaining instead of the original volume.

questions.stem: When liquid air is fractionally distilled, nitrogen boils off before oxygen because nitrogen
questions.explanation:
Nitrogen boils at −196 °C and oxygen at −183 °C, so nitrogen vaporises first as the liquid air warms.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- is less dense than oxygen: Separation depends on boiling point, not density.
- is more abundant in air: The amount present does not decide the order of boiling.
- is less reactive than oxygen: Reactivity does not affect distillation.

questions.stem: Iron rusts only when it is in contact with
questions.explanation:
Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O; salt water and acids speed up rusting.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- oxygen alone: Iron in dry air does not rust.
- water alone: Iron in boiled water under oil (no oxygen) does not rust.
- carbon(IV) oxide alone: Carbon(IV) oxide is not needed for rusting.

questions.stem: Electric light bulbs are filled with argon because argon
questions.explanation:
In air the hot tungsten filament would burn; argon, a noble gas, protects it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- burns brightly: Argon does not burn.
- conducts electricity: The filament conducts; the gas must not react with it.
- is the most abundant gas in air: Argon is less than 1% of air; nitrogen is the most abundant.

options.label: A
options.content: is unreactive and does not react with the hot filament

options.label: D
options.content: is the most abundant gas in air

papers.title: The Halogens: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the halogens, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In the laboratory preparation of chlorine from concentrated hydrochloric acid and manganese(IV) oxide, the manganese(IV) oxide acts as
questions.explanation:
MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O. Chloride ions are oxidised to chlorine; Mn is reduced from +4 to +2.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a catalyst: Manganese(IV) oxide is used up: it is reduced to manganese(II) chloride.
- a drying agent: Concentrated sulphuric acid dries the chlorine.
- a reducing agent: It removes electrons from chloride ions; it is the oxidising agent.

questions.stem: Chlorine prepared in the laboratory is passed first through water and then through concentrated sulphuric acid. The water removes
questions.explanation:
Hydrogen chloride from the acid is very soluble in water, while chlorine is only slightly soluble.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- water vapour: Concentrated sulphuric acid removes the water vapour.
- oxygen: No oxygen is produced in the preparation.
- manganese(II) chloride: Manganese(II) chloride stays in the flask.

questions.stem: When chlorine water is added to colourless potassium bromide solution, the solution turns
questions.explanation:
Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂. A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salts.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- violet, because iodine is displaced: There is no iodide in the solution.
- colourless, because no reaction takes place: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces it.
- pale green, because chlorine dissolves: The orange colour of bromine is seen.

options.label: B
options.content: colourless, because no reaction takes place

questions.stem: Going down group VII from fluorine to iodine,
questions.explanation:
Larger atoms attract an extra electron less strongly, so the halogens become weaker oxidising agents.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the boiling points decrease: Boiling points increase: fluorine and chlorine are gases, iodine is a solid.
- the colours become lighter: The colours darken: pale yellow, yellow-green, red-brown, black.
- the reactivity of the elements increases: Reactivity decreases down group VII.

options.label: A
options.content: the oxidising power of the elements decreases

options.label: D
options.content: the reactivity of the elements increases

questions.stem: Dry chlorine does not bleach dry litmus paper, but moist chlorine does, because
questions.explanation:
Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl; HOCl releases oxygen that oxidises the dye to a colourless substance.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- dry chlorine is not acidic: The bleaching is by oxidation, not acidity.
- water makes the chlorine more concentrated: Water does not concentrate chlorine.
- dry litmus paper is not coloured: Dry litmus is coloured; the chlorine needs water to bleach it.

options.label: B
options.content: water reacts with chlorine to form chloric(I) acid, which bleaches

options.label: C
options.content: water makes the chlorine more concentrated

options.label: D
options.content: dry litmus paper is not coloured

papers.title: Nitrogen and Its Compounds: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on nitrogen and its compounds, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which conditions are used in the Haber process for making ammonia?
questions.explanation:
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. High pressure favours ammonia; 450 °C with an iron catalyst gives a reasonable rate.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Vanadium(V) oxide catalyst, about 450 °C, 1–2 atm: These are the conditions of the Contact process.
- Platinum catalyst, about 900 °C, about 10 atm: These are the conditions of the Ostwald process.
- Nickel catalyst, about 150 °C, about 5 atm: These are conditions for hydrogenating vegetable oils.

questions.stem: Ammonia gas is dried by passing it through
questions.explanation:
Quicklime is a basic drying agent, so it removes water without reacting with the alkaline gas.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- concentrated sulphuric acid: Ammonia is alkaline and reacts with the acid to form ammonium sulphate.
- anhydrous calcium chloride: Ammonia combines with calcium chloride.
- phosphorus(V) oxide: This acidic drying agent reacts with ammonia.

questions.stem: In the fountain experiment, water rushes into a flask of ammonia and the red litmus in it turns blue. This shows that ammonia is
questions.explanation:
As ammonia dissolves, the pressure in the flask falls and water is pushed in: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- insoluble in water and acidic: The water rushes in because the gas dissolves rapidly.
- denser than air: Ammonia is less dense than air; density does not cause the fountain.
- a strong oxidising agent: The fountain shows solubility, not oxidising power.

options.label: A
options.content: very soluble in water and forms an alkaline solution

questions.stem: What is the percentage by mass of nitrogen in urea, CO(NH₂)₂? (Mᵣ = 60)
questions.explanation:
Mass of N $= 2 \times 14 = 28$; $\% \text{N} = \dfrac{28}{60} \times 100 = 46.7\%$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 23.33%: You counted only one nitrogen atom; urea has two.
- 28%: 28 is the mass of nitrogen in one molecule, not a percentage.
- 35%: 35% is the nitrogen content of ammonium nitrate, not urea.

questions.stem: When sodium nitrate is heated strongly, the products are
questions.explanation:
2NaNO₃ → 2NaNO₂ + O₂. Nitrates of very reactive metals (K, Na) give the nitrite and oxygen only.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- sodium oxide, nitrogen(IV) oxide and oxygen: That pattern applies to nitrates of metals below sodium, e.g. lead(II) nitrate.
- sodium and nitrogen: Heating does not break the salt into its elements.
- sodium oxide and nitrogen(IV) oxide only: Sodium nitrate gives no brown gas.

options.label: A
options.content: sodium oxide, nitrogen(IV) oxide and oxygen

options.label: D
options.content: sodium oxide and nitrogen(IV) oxide only

papers.title: Sulphur and Its Compounds: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on sulphur and its compounds, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The catalyst used in the Contact process is
questions.explanation:
2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ over V₂O₅ at about 450 °C and 1–2 atm.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- iron: Iron is the catalyst in the Haber process.
- platinum–rhodium: Platinum–rhodium is used in the Ostwald process.
- nickel: Nickel is used to hydrogenate oils.

questions.stem: In the Contact process, sulphur(VI) oxide is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid rather than in water because with water it
questions.explanation:
SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇ (oleum), which is then diluted carefully: H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- does not react: SO₃ reacts very vigorously with water.
- forms sulphuric(IV) acid: SO₃ with water gives sulphuric(VI) acid, but as an uncontrollable mist.
- explodes: The problem is the acid mist, not an explosion.

options.label: D
options.content: forms a fine mist of acid that is hard to collect

questions.stem: When concentrated sulphuric acid is added to sugar, a black mass of carbon forms. Here the acid acts as
questions.explanation:
C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ → 12C + 11H₂O: the acid removes the elements of water from the sugar.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- an oxidising agent: The acid removes hydrogen and oxygen as water; that is dehydration.
- a catalyst: The acid is used up as it absorbs the water.
- a reducing agent: Concentrated sulphuric acid is never a reducing agent.

questions.stem: Sulphur(IV) oxide bleaches damp coloured flowers by
questions.explanation:
SO₂ removes oxygen from the dye; air slowly re-oxidises it, so the colour can return (temporary bleaching).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- oxidation: Chlorine bleaches by oxidation; sulphur(IV) oxide bleaches by reduction.
- dehydration: Dehydration removes water; it does not bleach dyes.
- neutralisation: Bleaching is not an acid–base reaction.

questions.stem: In the Contact process each sulphur atom ends up in one H₂SO₄ molecule. What mass of sulphuric(VI) acid can be made from 32 g of sulphur? (H₂SO₄ = 98)
questions.explanation:
S → SO₂ → SO₃ → H₂SO₄: 1 mol S (32 g) gives 1 mol H₂SO₄ $= 98$ g.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 32 g: That is the mass of sulphur, not of the acid.
- 64 g: That is the mass of SO₂ formed in the first step.
- 80 g: That is the mass of SO₃, before it is converted into acid.

papers.title: Carbon and Its Inorganic Compounds: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on carbon and its inorganic compounds, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Diamond is very hard because
questions.explanation:
Every atom is held in place by strong C–C bonds in three dimensions, so the crystal is extremely hard.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- its atoms are held by weak van der Waals forces: Weak forces hold the layers of graphite, which is soft.
- it contains delocalised electrons: Diamond has no delocalised electrons; that is why it does not conduct.
- it is made of small carbon molecules: Diamond is a giant covalent structure, not molecular.

options.label: A
options.content: its atoms are held by weak van der Waals forces

options.label: C
options.content: each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a giant network

options.label: D
options.content: it is made of small carbon molecules

questions.stem: Graphite conducts electricity because
questions.explanation:
Three electrons form bonds within a layer; the fourth is delocalised and carries current along the layers.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- it contains carbon ions: Graphite is covalent; it has no ions.
- its layers slide over one another: Sliding layers make graphite soft and slippery, not conducting.
- each carbon atom forms four bonds: Each atom forms only three bonds in graphite; the fourth electron is free.

options.label: B
options.content: its layers slide over one another

options.label: C
options.content: each carbon atom forms four bonds

options.label: D
options.content: each carbon atom has one delocalised electron that moves between the layers

questions.stem: Dilute sulphuric acid is not used with marble chips to prepare carbon(IV) oxide because
questions.explanation:
Dilute hydrochloric acid is used instead: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂; calcium chloride is soluble.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- sulphuric acid does not react with carbonates: It does react at first, until the coating forms.
- the gas produced is sulphur(IV) oxide: The gas would still be carbon(IV) oxide.
- the reaction is too violent: The reaction quickly slows and stops.

options.label: A
options.content: insoluble calcium sulphate coats the marble and stops the reaction

options.label: B
options.content: sulphuric acid does not react with carbonates

options.label: C
options.content: the gas produced is sulphur(IV) oxide

questions.stem: Lime water turns milky when carbon(IV) oxide is bubbled through it, but clear again with excess gas, because
questions.explanation:
Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O, then CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ → Ca(HCO₃)₂(aq).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the calcium carbonate decomposes: Calcium carbonate decomposes only on strong heating.
- the water evaporates: The solution does not evaporate.
- calcium hydroxide is formed again: Excess CO₂ forms Ca(HCO₃)₂, not Ca(OH)₂.

questions.stem: What volume of carbon(IV) oxide at s.t.p. is given off when 10 g of calcium carbonate reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid? (CaCO₃ = 100)
questions.explanation:
Moles CaCO₃ $= \dfrac{10}{100} = 0.1$; moles CO₂ $= 0.1$; volume $= 0.1 \times 22.4 = 2.24$ dm³

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 22.4 dm³: You used the molar volume without finding the number of moles.
- 4.48 dm³: You used the 2 from 2HCl; 1 mol CaCO₃ gives 1 mol CO₂.
- 2.4 dm³: You used 24 dm³, the molar volume at room conditions.

papers.topic: Reactivity Series and Extraction of Metals
papers.title: Reactivity Series and Extraction of Metals: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on reactivity series and extraction of metals, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis rather than by heating its oxide with carbon because aluminium
questions.explanation:
Metals above carbon in the reactivity series (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) hold oxygen too strongly for carbon to remove it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- has a very low melting point: Its melting point does not decide the method; its reactivity does.
- does not form an oxide: Its ore, bauxite, is aluminium oxide.
- is found uncombined in nature: Aluminium is always found combined.

options.label: A
options.content: has a very low melting point

options.label: C
options.content: is too reactive to be reduced by carbon

questions.stem: The main reducing agent in the blast furnace is
questions.explanation:
Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. The CO is formed when coke burns and the CO₂ reacts with more coke.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- limestone: Limestone removes impurities as slag.
- hot air: Hot air burns the coke to provide heat and carbon(II) oxide.
- carbon(IV) oxide: Carbon(IV) oxide is reduced to carbon(II) oxide by coke; it does not reduce the ore.

questions.stem: Limestone is added to the blast furnace in order to
questions.explanation:
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, then CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (slag), which floats on the molten iron.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- reduce the iron ore: Carbon(II) oxide reduces the ore.
- provide oxygen for burning the coke: Hot air provides the oxygen.
- make the iron harder: Limestone does not dissolve in the iron.

options.label: C
options.content: provide oxygen for burning the coke

questions.stem: Which of the following mixtures will react?
questions.explanation:
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Copper and zinc sulphate solution: Copper is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot displace it.
- Silver and copper(II) sulphate solution: Silver is less reactive than copper.
- Iron and magnesium chloride solution: Iron is less reactive than magnesium.

questions.stem: What mass of iron can be obtained from 320 g of iron(III) oxide? Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (Fe₂O₃ = 160)
questions.explanation:
Moles Fe₂O₃ $= \dfrac{320}{160} = 2$; moles Fe $= 4$; mass $= 4 \times 56 = 224$ g

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 112 g: You used one mole of iron per mole of oxide; each Fe₂O₃ contains two Fe.
- 320 g: Mass is lost as oxygen is removed.
- 96 g: That is the mass of oxygen removed.

papers.title: Alkali Metals: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on alkali metals, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Sodium is stored under paraffin oil because it
questions.explanation:
Paraffin oil keeps out air and moisture; sodium would otherwise tarnish at once and react with water vapour.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- is very heavy: Sodium is less dense than water.
- melts at room temperature: Sodium melts at 98 °C.
- is poisonous: The reason is reactivity, not toxicity.

options.label: C
options.content: reacts rapidly with air and water

questions.stem: The products of the reaction of sodium with cold water are
questions.explanation:
2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. The sodium melts into a ball and darts about on the water.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- sodium oxide and hydrogen: The oxide reacts with water; the product in solution is the hydroxide.
- sodium hydroxide and oxygen: Water is reduced to hydrogen, not oxidised to oxygen.
- sodium oxide and oxygen: No oxygen is formed.

questions.stem: What colour does potassium give in a flame test?
questions.explanation:
Potassium's lilac flame is easily masked by sodium's yellow, so it is viewed through blue cobalt glass.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Golden yellow: Golden yellow is sodium.
- Brick-red: Brick-red is calcium.
- Blue-green: Blue-green is copper.

questions.stem: What volume of hydrogen at s.t.p. is produced when 2.3 g of sodium reacts completely with water? 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
questions.explanation:
Moles Na $= \dfrac{2.3}{23} = 0.1$; moles H₂ $= 0.05$; volume $= 0.05 \times 22.4 = 1.12$ dm³

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2.24 dm³: You used a 1 : 1 ratio; 2 mol Na give 1 mol H₂.
- 4.48 dm³: You doubled the moles instead of halving them.
- 1.2 dm³: You used 24 dm³, the molar volume at room conditions.

questions.stem: Sodium carbonate is manufactured industrially by
questions.explanation:
The Solvay process uses brine, limestone and ammonia; sodium hydrogencarbonate is heated to give sodium carbonate.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the Haber process: The Haber process makes ammonia.
- the Contact process: The Contact process makes sulphuric(VI) acid.
- the Ostwald process: The Ostwald process makes nitric(V) acid.

papers.title: Alkaline Earth Metals: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on alkaline earth metals, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Magnesium ribbon burns in air with
questions.explanation:
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO; some magnesium nitride, Mg₃N₂, also forms with the nitrogen in air.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a lilac flame, forming a black powder: Lilac is potassium's flame colour; MgO is white.
- a pale blue flame, forming a yellow liquid: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white light.
- no flame, because magnesium is unreactive: Magnesium burns readily once lit.

options.label: A
options.content: a lilac flame, forming a black powder

options.label: B
options.content: a pale blue flame, forming a yellow liquid

options.label: C
options.content: a brilliant white flame, forming a white powder

options.label: D
options.content: no flame, because magnesium is unreactive

questions.stem: Calcium reacts with cold water to give
questions.explanation:
Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. Calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble, so the mixture looks milky.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- oxygen and calcium oxide: Water is reduced to hydrogen; no oxygen forms.
- hydrogen and calcium carbonate: There is no carbon in the reactants.
- no reaction: Calcium reacts steadily with cold water.

options.label: D
options.content: hydrogen and a milky suspension of calcium hydroxide

questions.stem: When limestone (calcium carbonate) is heated strongly in a kiln, it forms
questions.explanation:
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Quicklime (CaO) is used to make cement, slaked lime and in steel-making.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- calcium hydroxide and carbon(IV) oxide: Calcium hydroxide forms when water is added to quicklime.
- calcium and carbon(IV) oxide: Heating does not release the metal.
- calcium oxide and carbon(II) oxide: The gas is carbon(IV) oxide.

questions.stem: Farmers add slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂, to soil in order to
questions.explanation:
Calcium hydroxide neutralises acids in the soil, raising the pH so that crops grow better.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increase the nitrogen content: Slaked lime contains no nitrogen.
- make the soil more acidic: Slaked lime is a base; it neutralises acids.
- kill all insects: Liming is not a pesticide treatment.

options.label: B
options.content: reduce the acidity of the soil

questions.stem: Which compound is used to make casts for broken bones?
questions.explanation:
Plaster of Paris mixed with water sets hard as it forms gypsum, CaSO₄·2H₂O.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂: Slaked lime is used in mortar and to treat acidic soil.
- Quicklime, CaO: Quicklime reacts violently with water and would burn the skin.
- Limestone, CaCO₃: Limestone does not set when mixed with water.

papers.title: Aluminium and Group III Metals: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on aluminium and group iii metals, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The chief ore of aluminium is
questions.explanation:
Bauxite is impure hydrated aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃·2H₂O; Sierra Leone has bauxite deposits in the south.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- haematite: Haematite is an ore of iron.
- cryolite: Cryolite is added to lower the melting point; it is not the main ore.
- rutile: Rutile is an ore of titanium.

questions.stem: Cryolite is added in the electrolytic extraction of aluminium in order to
questions.explanation:
Pure Al₂O₃ melts at about 2050 °C; dissolved in molten cryolite it can be electrolysed at about 950 °C.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- act as the anode: The anodes are made of carbon.
- reduce the aluminium ions: Aluminium ions are reduced by electrons at the cathode.
- increase the amount of oxygen produced: Cryolite does not change the products.

options.label: A
options.content: lower the melting point of the electrolyte and save energy

options.label: D
options.content: increase the amount of oxygen produced

questions.stem: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series, yet aluminium roofing sheets do not corrode because
questions.explanation:
The oxide layer is tough and sticks to the metal, so air and water cannot reach the aluminium beneath.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- aluminium is less reactive than iron: Aluminium is more reactive than iron.
- aluminium does not react with oxygen: Aluminium reacts with oxygen at once to form the protective oxide.
- rain water contains no oxygen: Rain water contains dissolved oxygen.

options.label: A
options.content: aluminium is less reactive than iron

options.label: B
options.content: a thin, unreactive layer of aluminium oxide protects the metal

options.label: C
options.content: aluminium does not react with oxygen

questions.stem: What mass of aluminium is deposited at the cathode by 289 500 C of electricity? Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (Al = 27; F = 96 500 C/mol)
questions.explanation:
Moles of electrons $= \dfrac{289\,500}{96\,500} = 3$; moles Al $= \dfrac{3}{3} = 1$; mass $= 27$ g

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 81 g: You used one electron per aluminium ion; three are needed.
- 40.5 g: You used two electrons per aluminium ion.
- 3 g: That is the number of moles of electrons, not the mass of aluminium.

questions.stem: Aluminium hydroxide dissolves in both dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution. This shows that it is
questions.explanation:
Al(OH)₃ + 3HCl → AlCl₃ + 3H₂O and Al(OH)₃ + NaOH → NaAl(OH)₄ (sodium aluminate).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- basic only: A purely basic hydroxide would not dissolve in sodium hydroxide.
- acidic only: A purely acidic hydroxide would not dissolve in hydrochloric acid.
- neutral: A neutral substance reacts with neither.

papers.title: Iron and Other Transition Metals: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on iron and other transition metals, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A solution containing iron(II) ions gives, with sodium hydroxide solution,
questions.explanation:
Fe²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₂(s); the green precipitate slowly turns brown in air as it is oxidised.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a red-brown precipitate: That is iron(III) hydroxide, from Fe³⁺ ions.
- a blue precipitate: That is copper(II) hydroxide.
- a white precipitate that dissolves in excess: That is zinc, aluminium or lead hydroxide.

options.label: C
options.content: a white precipitate that dissolves in excess

questions.stem: Rust is
questions.explanation:
Rust is Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. It flakes off, so fresh iron below is exposed and rusting continues.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- iron(II) oxide: Rust contains iron in the +3 state and water.
- anhydrous iron(III) oxide: Rust contains water of hydration.
- iron(II) carbonate: Rust is an oxide, not a carbonate.

questions.stem: Which pair of properties is typical of transition metals?
questions.explanation:
Iron forms Fe²⁺ (green) and Fe³⁺ (yellow-brown); copper forms Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺ (blue). Many also act as catalysts.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Low melting points and low densities: Transition metals are hard, dense and high-melting.
- One oxidation state and white compounds: These are typical of group I and II metals.
- Very vigorous reactions with cold water: Transition metals react slowly, if at all, with water.

options.label: A
options.content: Low melting points and low densities

options.label: B
options.content: Variable oxidation states and coloured compounds

options.label: C
options.content: One oxidation state and white compounds

options.label: D
options.content: Very vigorous reactions with cold water

questions.stem: Steel is made from pig iron mainly by
questions.explanation:
Pig iron contains about 4% carbon, which makes it brittle. Oxygen burns off carbon as CO₂ and other impurities form slag.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- adding more coke to the molten iron: Coke would add carbon; steel needs less carbon.
- electrolysing the molten iron: Iron is not refined by electrolysis.
- heating the iron with limestone only: Limestone removes silica; oxygen removes carbon.

options.label: A
options.content: adding more coke to the molten iron

options.label: C
options.content: blowing oxygen through the molten iron to remove most of the carbon

options.label: D
options.content: heating the iron with limestone only

questions.stem: Excess ammonia solution added to a solution of copper(II) ions gives
questions.explanation:
A blue precipitate of Cu(OH)₂ forms first, then dissolves in excess ammonia to give the deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ ion.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a red-brown precipitate: That is iron(III) hydroxide.
- a white precipitate: Copper(II) hydroxide is blue, not white.
- a green solution: Copper ions with ammonia are deep blue.

papers.title: Industrial Chemical Processes: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on industrial chemical processes, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The most important factor in deciding where to site a cement factory is nearness to
questions.explanation:
Cement factories use huge amounts of heavy limestone; siting them near the quarry cuts transport costs.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a large river for shipping: Transport matters, but limestone is bulky and is the main raw material.
- a big city market: The raw material is far heavier and bulkier than the product.
- an international airport: Air transport is not used for cement.

questions.stem: The catalyst used for oxidising ammonia in the manufacture of nitric(V) acid is
questions.explanation:
Ostwald process: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O over Pt–Rh at about 900 °C; NO is then oxidised and absorbed in water.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- finely divided iron: Iron is the Haber process catalyst.
- vanadium(V) oxide: Vanadium(V) oxide is the Contact process catalyst.
- nickel: Nickel is used for hydrogenating oils.

questions.stem: In the Haber process, the nitrogen and hydrogen that do not react are
questions.explanation:
Only about 15% conversion happens each pass, so recycling gives an overall yield of about 98%.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- released into the air: That would waste raw materials.
- burned to provide heat: Nitrogen does not burn; the gases are reused.
- dissolved in water: Ammonia is removed by cooling; the unreacted gases are recycled.

questions.stem: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. What volume of ammonia is formed if 30 dm³ of hydrogen reacts completely with nitrogen (same temperature and pressure)?
questions.explanation:
By Gay-Lussac's law, volume of NH₃ $= 30 \times \dfrac{2}{3} = 20$ dm³

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 45 dm³: You inverted the ratio; 3 volumes of hydrogen give 2 volumes of ammonia.
- 10 dm³: That is the volume of nitrogen used.
- 30 dm³: You assumed a 1 : 1 ratio.

questions.stem: The Haber process is run at about 450 °C, although a lower temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield of ammonia, because at a lower temperature
questions.explanation:
450 °C is a compromise between a reasonable yield and a fast enough rate.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the catalyst would be poisoned: Catalyst poisoning is caused by impurities, not low temperature.
- ammonia would decompose: Ammonia is more stable at lower temperatures.
- the pressure would fall to zero: Pressure is set by the compressors, not by the temperature.

options.label: C
options.content: the pressure would fall to zero

options.label: D
options.content: the reaction would be too slow
